content:
Hi, I think I may have posted this in the wrong stream a moment ago, so let me ask the narrower question directly.

I’m looking for advice on how to ensure that I am not unintentionally introducing structure or assumptions in a larger Lean 4 development, even when the resulting theorems appear axiom-free under tools like #print axioms.

In particular, I’m worried about hidden force coming from definitional packaging, imported infrastructure, typeclass machinery, or kernel-level assumptions that I may not be accounting for correctly. I’ve avoided importing mathlib and propext, but I would really appreciate guidance on the right way to audit this rigorously.

Thanks,
Charles
If #print axioms doesn't show new axioms and the proof compiles, you're essentially good. If you want to triple check, though, you can use comparator https://github.com/leanprover/comparator.
Note that the real difficulty is to check that the statement is indeed saying what you think it says (in particular for definitions)

Thank you, I will take a look.

Note that the real difficulty is to check that the statement is indeed saying what you think it says (in particular for definitions)

That is exactly where I am struggling, frankly.
Note that #print axioms will not save you from AI adding lemmas that aren’t used in your main theorems.
It will also not save you from bad definitions that AI might add and use directly or indirectly in your theorem statements.

Thank you, that's also a good point... I was having trouble in anchroing a latex draft in only the lean definitions that I needed. I tagged equations with a macro \lean, with the lean definition name. But, trimming the 'bloat' was maddening, and in the end... I have a bunch that builds, with im sure bloat.

It would be nice if there was a way to anchor a latex document with lean. And invert that, find what in the lean is not needed in the paper, to help audit it by hand.
Another issue you might face if you ask AI to document your proof in a paper is that it might blatantly lie about the proof structure that it actually uses.

so, I'm not one to say that anything written by AI is what AI claims it is (in general). I think AI currently has this view that any lean code written that builds is irrefutable, without the nuance of where you can abuse it. And that's what I'm coming to terms with.

I think one source of confidence in a lemma's statement comes from using it to prove other related statements. If it integrates well into the broader theory, it's less probable to make mistakes. In my understanding, that's one reason why there's few doubt about the statements in mathlib; they usually come with a whole surrounding theory.

Paul Reichert said:

In my understanding, that's one reason why there's few doubt about the statements in mathlib; they usually come with a whole surrounding theory.

I think, if I did it right, I have some 2k+ from just the three, all building off each other, with almost all having 'does not depend on any axioms', and a few depending on my three.

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

Note that the real difficulty is to check that the statement is indeed saying what you think it says (in particular for definitions)

My take on this is that I need external unbiased eyes on it. What would be a good way to get that without shilling the work? I'm hoping to find a gross error that I'm missing that tears the whole thing down.

color me desperate lol, but incase i can get anyone to look, i'd love to know what i am missing... i've spent a long time try to find where this breaks and i cant. ... i have some 2,500 with no axioms needed almost entirely, definitions pinned to every equation in the paper with latex \lean tags ... the lean files are all there. I'm not sure what more I can do :)

Sébastien Gouëzel said:

If #print axioms doesn't show new axioms and the proof compiles, you're essentially good. If you want to triple check, though, you can use comparator https://github.com/leanprover/comparator.

Working on that now, thank you. But to your point about whether the statement is indeed saying what I think it says, yes, that is the hard part. I feel like I am in a bit of a circular loop defining the goal to verify a proof chain that gets the goal? My naive approach has been to try and build a separate one-way mathlib validation lane (just 153 theorems) to show that I can recover the standard Hilbert/operator structures from the three axioms. The idea being, I'm not choosing the goal there.

Well you are just one of many people on this Zulip instance saying "please read my AI-generated code for free and give me feedback" and unfortunately the community's patience with such requests seems to be wearing very thin.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Well you are just one of many people on this Zulip instance saying "please read my AI-generated code for free and give me feedback" and unfortunately the community's patience with such requests seems to be wearing very thin.

I absolutely get that... and trust me, I review pull requests all day from engineers using ai, and it's is taxing... I get it... they dont read the code they write... so the reviewer ends up do 10x the work so the dev can be 10x as productive.

I'm just looking for ways to sanity check im doing it right, not have someone review the lean itself.
I guess a bit more on the meta side... it feels a bit ironic that the machine verification doesnt mean much without a human verifying the machine is doing the right thing.

Your point @Kevin Buzzard is hitting pretty hard as I'm complaining about reviewing code from AI while being paid for it... is there an appropriate way to compensate someone for a review? I'm not trying to be cheap here.

@Charles Cook, the moment you write the word axiom, everything you have done is worthless. (That is not to say that axiom is not useful for some Lean users, but it is not useful to you.)

Moderator hat on: do not post about (or link to) projects that use the axiom keyword, again.
acknowledged... removed the link
Thank you for the feedback, Kim. I’ve updated the project so the project-owned Lean files now build cleanly without using the axiom keyword.
